Fact.Name: Printed "Died" literal in place of this person's number
Fact.Description:
The word the printed forms put in this person's identifying-number box when the person is a child born and died in the tax year with no TIN and the taxpayer holds the document the instructions accept in the number's place (../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin). It resolves to nothing for everyone else, so a form field bound to this fact beside the number prints exactly one of the two.
THREE PRINTED BOXES ask for it, each in its own instruction: Form 1040 Dependents row (3); Schedule EIC line 2, Child's SSN; and Form 2441 line 2, column (b). This fact fills the first two; Form 2441 column (b) reaches the person through the child and dependent care credit's own rank chain and needs a rank-side literal beside it before it can print one. Each of the three also requires the birth certificate, death certificate or hospital records to be sent with the return, which is what ../writableBornAndDiedChildDocumentation attests.
WHY IT IS NOT ../mefDeceasedCode. That fact emits the MeF code for any person who is deceased and has no TIN, whoever they are and whenever they were born. The printed substitute is narrower: the instructions offer it only for a child BORN AND DIED IN THE SAME TAX YEAR whose documentation the taxpayer holds. A dependent born in an earlier year who died in this one, with no TIN, gets no substitute and no printed literal - this fact is Incomplete for that person while ../mefDeceasedCode is not.
SPELLING. Three of the four governing instructions print "Died" - the Form 1040 instructions for row (3), the Schedule EIC line-2 caption and the Form 2441 line-2 instruction - and this fact carries that spelling. Publication 501 prints "DIED" for the same box and MeF's DiedLiteralCd is an all-capitals schema value, so the printed word and the transmitted code differ in case on purpose.

The person was born and died in the tax year, and never received a TIN.
This fact is NOT the refusal itself. It is the ASKED-WHEN gate for ../writableBornAndDiedChildDocumentation and the first leg of ../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin; the refusal moved to ../bornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTinUndocumented, which is this test AND no documentation. Exported downstream so the application can gate the screen on it. The binary attachment and the MeF DiedLiteralCd are not built.

Fact.Name: Documentation held for a child born and died in the tax year
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's attestation that they hold the document Pub. 501 and the Form 1040 instructions accept in place of a missing SSN for a child born and died in the tax year. A Yes is also what puts the word in the number's place on the printed return: ../diedLiteralInLieuOfTin carries the literal the instructions print, and ../mefDeceasedCode carries the separate all-capitals MeF code.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION - the application implements this without opening a statute.
SCREEN NAME (proposed): BornAndDiedChildDocumentation, in the Dependents section, immediately after the TIN question for this person (the screen that would otherwise dead-end in a knockout) and before the person's summary.
QUESTION TEXT, as asked, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "Do you have a copy of {name}'s birth certificate, death certificate, or hospital records to include with your return?"
HELP TEXT, paraphrasing the governing instruction: "Because {name} was born and died in 2025 and does not have a Social Security number, the IRS lets you send a copy of {name}'s birth certificate, death certificate, or hospital records instead of a number. The document has to show that the child was born alive. If you do this, "DIED" goes in the Social Security number space of the Dependents section instead of a number. Answer Yes only if you have one of those documents now." Sources: Publication 501, Born and died in 2025 - "If your child was born and died in 2025, and you don't have an SSN for the child, you may attach a copy of the child's birth certificate, death certificate, or hospital records instead. The document must show the child was born alive. If you do this, enter "DIED" in row (3) of the Dependents section of your Form 1040 or 1040-SR" - https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p501.pdf, page 23 (a three-column extraction, so the sentence runs down alternating lines); and the 2025 Instructions for Form 1040, Dependents - https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 22, RIGHT column.
ASKED WHEN: ../bornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin is true for this person - born in the tax year, died in the tax year, and ../tinType answered "none". Ask it ONCE PER PERSON; the household can hold more than one such child and the answers are independent. Do NOT ask it of a child who died in the tax year but was born earlier: the printed substitute is written only for born-AND-died.
UNANSWERED POSTURE, and why. Unanswered means NO. ../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin gates this writable on its own IsComplete, so an unanswered screen reads Complete false and BOTH /knockoutPersonBornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin and /knockoutHohQpHasNoTin keep refusing exactly the filers they refuse today. That is deliberate: with no document there is nothing to put in the number's place, so the safe reading of silence is "we do not have it". There is no Placeholder and no default.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, labels "Yes" / "No", no default selection, answer required to leave the screen. No Min/Max. The document itself is NOT uploaded here - this writable records only that it exists; the upload belongs to the MeF binary-attachment surface below.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin (per person) and /bornAndDiedChildDocumentationInLieuOfTin (the return-level roll-up), and through them ../eligibleDependentMinusFilerInformation (the dependency claim), the head-of-household qualifying-person chain, ../cdccQualifyingPerson, and the narrowing of both knockouts in flow.xml. A Yes lets the return claim the child as a dependent and, where the child is the only head-of-household qualifying person, lets the filer keep that status. It also lets the child count as a qualifying person for the child and dependent care credit: the Form 2441 instructions print the same substitute for the qualifying person's number ("Died" in column (b), with the record attached), which answers IRC 21(e)(10). It does NOT reach the CTC (IRC 24(h)(7), SSN), the ODC (IRC 24(e)(1), TIN) or the EITC amount (IRC 32(m), SSN) - each is separately gated and the tests assert those negatives.
ORDERING, AND THE GRAPH ENFORCES IT. ../writableBornOrDiedLivedWithTpMostOfLife should be wired in the same release, and if it is not, nothing breaks: this screen's Yes alone does NOT retire /knockoutPersonBornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin, because ../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin also requires that the residency question have been ANSWERED. Wiring this screen without the other one therefore leaves the refusal standing - a safe ordering, not a hazard. MeF FOLLOW-ON (named, not built here): a Yes means the return must carry the child's document as an MeF binary attachment and put the DIED literal in the dependent's SSN position. The two facts this writable feeds deliberately do NOT carry Export mef - no MeF schema is vendored in this repo, so the elements are named in the records overlay for the binding unit to verify and bind, rather than asserted here by an export that names nothing.

Fact.Name: Born-and-died child claimed on documentation instead of a TIN
Fact.Description:
Per person: this child was born and died in the tax year with no TIN, AND the taxpayer holds the documentation Pub. 501 accepts in place of the number. That combination is a claimable dependent on the printed route, which is why ../eligibleDependentMinusFilerInformation reads it as the alternative to a TIN and why /knockoutHohQpHasNoTin no longer refuses a filer whose only head-of-household qualifying person is this child.
WHICH BENEFITS IT REACHES, decided against each benefit's OWN identification requirement rather than by analogy: DEPENDENCY CLAIM - YES. Pub. 501 and i1040gi print the documentation route about the dependents section itself, and IRC 151(e)'s TIN condition is what the printed substitute answers. HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD - YES. IRC 2(b) states no TIN condition, and Pub. 501 Table 4 makes a claimed unmarried qualifying child a qualifying person. CTC - NO. IRC 24(h)(7) needs a social security number; ../eligibleCtc already requires ../tinType = ssn, so this arm cannot reach it and no edit was needed there. ODC - NO. IRC 24(e)(1) bars any section 24 credit for a qualifying child whose TIN is not on the return. ../eligibleOdc did not test the TIN because ../isClaimedDependent implied one; the condition is added there. CDCC - YES. IRC 21(e)(10) requires the qualifying individual's TIN on the return, and the Form 2441 instructions print this substitute for that entry: "If the child was born and died in 2025 and didn't have an SSN, enter "Died" in column (b) and attach a copy of the child's birth certificate, death certificate, or hospital medical records" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3, right column). Every arm of ../cdccQualifyingPerson and ../cdccNonDependentQualifyingPerson reads this fact as the alternative to a TIN. The literal itself is ../diedLiteralInLieuOfTin, which is bound beside the number on Form 1040 row (3) and Schedule EIC line 2. Form 2441 line 2 column (b) is NOT bound to it yet: /form2441Line2Row1Tin and its row siblings reach the person through the cdcc rank chain (/cdccLine2PersonRank1Tin reads /cdccLine2QualifyingPersonAtRankMax1Item0/tin), so that column needs a rank-side literal of its own and prints no number for this child until it has one. EITC - YES, for the credit AMOUNT as well as for eligibility. The statute alone would say NO for the credit AMOUNT - IRC 32(c)(3)(D) with 32(m) counts only an SSA-issued SSN. But Publication 596 prints the SAME documented exception the dependents section gets, in the same CAUTION that states the SSN rule: "To claim a higher EIC amount based on a qualifying child, that qualifying child must have a valid SSN issued on or before the due date of your 2025 return (including extensions), unless the child was born and died in 2025 and you attach to your return a copy of the child's birth certificate, death certificate, or hospital records showing a live birth" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p596.pdf, page 13, RIGHT column), and Schedule EIC line 2's own caption carries it - "unless the child was born and died in 2025 or you are claiming the self-only EIC" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sei.pdf, page 1), which is the only reason "Died" goes on that line at all. THE FOOTING IS THE ONE THIS WHOLE ARM ALREADY STANDS ON: IRC 151(e) carries no born-and-died exception either, yet the instructions print one for row (3) and this dictionary computes it. Reading the statute over the instruction here and the instruction over the statute three lines up would be incoherent. So ../eitcQualifyingChildForCalculation takes the documented child on a disjunct beside ../ssnValidForEITCCalculation. An UNDOCUMENTED child without an SSN still gets no amount - that is the self-only EIC path, and it is the witness that keeps the two apart.
THE RESIDENCY ANSWER IS A PRECONDITION, ENFORCED HERE. This fact reads false until ../writableBornOrDiedLivedWithTpMostOfLife has been ANSWERED - either way. The claim it unblocks needs the born-or-died residency exception as well as the document, so switching the guard off on the document alone would deny the dependency claim and head of household silently in any release that wired one screen and not the other. Gating on IsComplete of the WRITABLE separates "we did not ask" (refuse) from "we asked and the answer is no" (compute, and correctly deny); the two were byte-identical before this conjunct.
COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION, which is why consumers read it bare. Every leg is gated on its own IsComplete, so an unanswered date of birth, an unanswered deceased flag, an unanswered documentation answer or an unasked residency-exception screen all resolve to Complete false rather than Incomplete, and the two guards that negate it keep the completeness profile they have today.
MeF: this fact IS the per-dependent condition under which the dependent's SSN position carries the DIED literal (../mefDeceasedCode) and the return carries the child's document as a binary attachment - but it does NOT carry Export mef. No MeF schema is vendored in this repo, so the element this fact would feed cannot be named against an on-disk artifact. An export naming nothing is worse than none, and adding it would also move every committed spine TSV the moment the lead regenerates dictionary/manifest/facts-manifest.json - scripts/gen_spine.py:127 computes spine membership as (mef-exported union pinned core) intersect manifest_keys. The binding unit adds the flag with a verified element name.

Fact.Name: Born and died in the tax year, no TIN, and no documentation to put in its place
Fact.Description:
The NARROWED trigger of /knockoutPersonBornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin. The refusal used to fire on the whole born-and-died-without-a-TIN population; the printed documentation route for that population now computes, so what is left is the DATA-COMPLETENESS RESIDUE: the filer who has not said they hold the birth certificate, death certificate or hospital records the substitute requires. That residue is the correct permanent refusal - without the document there is nothing to put in row (3) but a blank - and it is the whole of what this guard now refuses.
NO COMMITTED SCENARIO MOVES. ../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin is Complete false on every scenario today (the intake is unasked), so this fact is exactly ../bornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin, with the same value AND the same completeness.

Fact.Name: The return claims a born-and-died child on documentation instead of a TIN
Fact.Description:
The return-level answer of the per-person /familyAndHousehold/*/bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin: at least one claimed household member is a child born and died in the tax year, with no TIN, for whom the taxpayer holds the Pub. 501 documentation. This is the fact the records contract names; the household can hold more than one such child, which is why the determination is per person and this is the roll-up.
WHAT IT IS FOR. It is the return-level flag the MeF surface needs: a return carrying it must transmit the binary attachment and set DiedLiteralCd beside the "DIED" literal this module already emits at /familyAndHousehold/*/mefDeceasedCode. MeF is in scope, but nothing in this dictionary reads this fact yet and it is exported downstream rather than left unwired. DELIBERATELY NOT Export mef: no MeF schema is vendored in this repo, so the return-level element this would feed cannot be named against an on-disk artifact, and an export naming nothing is worse than none.
The family/household member who caused the born and died in TY knockout

We should knockout the user because one of their family and household was born and died in the tax year without a TIN.
This does not refuse the whole born-and-died-without-a-TIN population: that population now has the printed documentation route (/familyAndHousehold/*/bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin, with the born-or-died residency exception at ../bornOrDiedResidencyException). WHAT IT NOW REFUSES is the residue named on /familyAndHousehold/*/bornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTinUndocumented - the child with NEITHER a TIN NOR the birth certificate, death certificate or hospital records the substitute requires, for whom there is nothing to put in row (3) but a blank. That is a data-completeness refusal and it is permanent.
The return-wide refusal is suppressed where the undocumented child is left out of the EIC count: every undocumented born-and-died child in this residue is an EITC qualifying child and none of them is counted toward the amount. Schedule EIC lists a child on line 2 only with an SSN, the born-and-died document, or on the self-only path, so such a child is on no printed row: with no child counted the return takes the self-only EIC the printed Schedule EIC permits, and with a counted sibling (a valid SSN, or a documented born-and-died child) the credit is figured on the counted children alone. The child's dependent claim remains false without the accepted documentation. Any undocumented child who is not an EITC qualifying child, or the independent head-of-household qualifying-person TIN refusal, keeps this knockout active.
The born-and-died EIC suppression is consulted only when the undocumented born-and-died count is above zero, the population it exists to suppress. Otherwise that leg is True and the knockout is its first leg alone, so a return with no such child does not wait on the family collection the suppression reads. A return whose family collection was never answered holds no child at all and reads Complete false before either leg. See the comment on the Derived body for the shape and for the one residue it does not close.

THE LOCAL-LAW RULE. IRC 21(e)(1): an individual is not treated as having the taxpayer's principal place of abode if at any time during the year the relationship between them is in violation of local law. Every route below rests on that shared abode (the qualifying child's residency, or the incapable person's living with the taxpayer), so a Yes to ../writableCdccRelationshipViolatesLocalLaw takes the person out of every route.

Fact.Name: Relationship with this person violated local law
Fact.Description:
Whether, at any time in 2025, the relationship between the taxpayer and this person was in violation of local law. IRC 21(e)(1) then treats the person as NOT sharing the taxpayer's principal place of abode, so the person cannot be a qualifying person for the child and dependent care credit (../cdccQualifyingPerson).
QUESTION TEXT: "At any time in 2025, was your relationship with this person against the law where you live?"
HELP TEXT: The credit counts a person who lived with you only if your relationship with them was lawful where you live for all of 2025. Most filers answer No.
THE SAME RULE FOR DEPENDENCY. IRC 152(f)(3) states it for the dependency tests: such a person is not a member of the taxpayer's household, so they cannot be a qualifying relative through the member-of-household route (../memberOfHouseholdTest). One question serves both rules: the fact the taxpayer attests is the same, so it is asked once per person.
ASKED WHEN: this person could qualify the taxpayer for the credit (../personCouldQualifyTPForCdcc) and the return claims care expenses; OR this person is not related to the taxpayer in one of the listed ways (dependentsRelationship:../qrRelationshipTest is false) and lived with the taxpayer all year, or was born or died during the year (the member-of-household route, the same population as ../writableWasSpouseAtAnyTimeInTaxYear). Ask it once per person.
UNANSWERED: the two readers differ because the question is reached differently. ../memberOfHouseholdTest reads it bare: the local-law rule is printed inside the member-of-household test itself, so while that route decides the outcome an unanswered screen leaves the test, and the qualifying-relative claim it feeds, Incomplete rather than granting a dependency the statute may deny. ../cdccQualifyingPerson reads it IsComplete-first: neither the Form 2441 instructions nor Publication 503 print the rule as a condition of a qualifying person, so for the credit an unasked question never removes a qualifying person.
VALIDATION: Boolean, Yes / No.
FEEDS: ../cdccQualifyingPerson, ../memberOfHouseholdTest.

Line 2 column (d): ../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, less any part of it the filer also included in Schedule A medical expenses (../writableCdccExpensesAlsoClaimedAsMedical, asked only where this person was physically or mentally unable to care for themselves and the return itemizes deductions with medical expenses on Schedule A), never below $0.

Fact.Name: Care expenses in this amount that were paid to a barred related care provider
Fact.Description:
The dollars of this person's care expenses (../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) that the filer paid to a care provider barred by IRC 21(e)(6) — the filer's spouse, the parent of the qualifying child, a person the filer or spouse can claim as a dependent, or the filer's own child who had not reached age 19 by the close of the year.
QUESTION TEXT: "You told us one of your care providers is someone the credit does not allow you to pay. How much of the care expenses you entered for this person did you pay to that provider?" (enter 0 if none of them).
HELP TEXT: the printed caution is the whole of the rule — "Don't list an ineligible related individual as a care provider on line 1. No credit is allowed for any amount paid to your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child, or a person whom you can claim as a dependent. If your child (including stepchild or foster child) provided the care, they must have been age 19 or older by the end of the year and they can't be your dependent" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3).
WHY THE QUESTION HANGS HERE AND NOT ON THE PROVIDER. The provider collection already carries a per-provider amount (cdcc:/cdccCareProviders/*/amountPaidForCare) but no link saying WHICH qualifying person that payment bought care for, and a provider's payment can also contain dollars that are not in the credit at all (care in another year, care that is not employment-related). Subtracting a provider's gross payment from an arbitrary person's expenses would remove allowed dollars; asking the allocation per person removes exactly the disallowed ones. This is shape (ii) of the two the rebody contract at cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider offered, chosen on the record for that reason.
ASKED WHEN: the return reports at least one barred provider (cdcc:/cdccCareProviders/*/writableIsBarredRelatedProvider true on some row) and this person has qualifying expenses (../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses).
UNANSWERED: on that population the return is REFUSED (cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider), which is the narrowed residue of the refusal that used to fire on every barred provider whether or not anything could be netted. Nothing is defaulted: a $0 default would let the disallowed dollars stay inside the credit silently. Where no provider is barred the question is never asked and nothing is subtracted.
VALIDATION: a dollar amount, not less than $0. An answer larger than the expense it is taken out of is floored rather than refused — the netted amount never goes below $0 — because over-answering can only reduce the credit, which is the taxpayer-adverse direction.
FEEDS: subtracted from ../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount inside ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, which is Form 2441 line 2 column (d). Because the subtraction lands in that wrapper rather than in the credit total, it reaches the more-than-three RANKING as well as the printed rows, line 3 and line 30: the person whose expenses were mostly paid to a barred provider stops out-ranking a person whose were not.

Fact.Name: Barred-provider dollars still inside this amount, complete-safe
Fact.Description:
../writableCdccBarredProviderExpensesStillIncluded behind the IsComplete/Switch idiom: the answered amount rounded and floored at $0, and $0 wherever the question was not asked or not answered. NOT a Placeholder: ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount subtracts this, and a Placeholder here would turn Form 2441 line 2 column (d) — and through it line 3, line 30 and the whole credit — Placeholder on every return in the corpus.
A $0 READ IS NOT A CLAIM THAT NOTHING WAS PAID TO A BARRED PROVIDER. It is safe only because cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider carries the answeredness test separately: a return with a barred provider and an unanswered allocation reads $0 here AND is refused.
The GreaterOf floor is not decoration: a Limit Min on a Writable is a write-time declaration and is not enforced on resolution, so a negative answer would otherwise ADD to the expense it is meant to remove.

Fact.Name: A barred-provider allocation this return still owes
Fact.Description:
TRUE exactly when this person has qualifying expenses and the barred-provider allocation is unanswered — the one condition cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider still refuses on after the netting landed.
IsComplete-FIRST ON BOTH LIMBS, so an unanswered ../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses reads Complete(false) here rather than spreading incompleteness into a BlockSubmissionOnTrue guard. A person with no qualifying expenses has no dollars to allocate and is never counted.

Fact.Name: Care expenses also included in Schedule A medical expenses
Fact.Description:
The dollars of this person's care expenses (../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) that the filer ALSO included in the medical expenses on Schedule A line 1.
QUESTION TEXT: "Did you include any of these care expenses in your medical expenses on Schedule A? If so, how much?" (enter 0 if none).
HELP TEXT: "You can't use the same expenses to claim both a credit and a medical expense deduction" (Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 10; Instructions for Form 2441, lines 124-130). Enter the part of the care expenses you entered for this person that is also in your Schedule A medical expenses; it is taken out of the expenses used for the credit. If your care expenses are more than the credit's limit (the dollar limit, $3,000 for one qualifying person or $6,000 for two or more, or your earned income if that is smaller), you can put the excess on Schedule A without lowering the credit; if you put all of them on Schedule A, none of them can be used for the credit (Pub. 503 lines 693-698).
ASKED WHEN: this person is a qualifying person for the credit (../cdccQualifyingPerson) who was physically or mentally unable to care for themselves (../unableToCareForSelf), AND the filer paid qualifying care expenses (../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses), AND the return itemizes deductions (taxCalculations:/wantsStandardDeduction false: Schedule A is claimed and either exceeds the standard deduction or the filer elects to itemize; Form 2441 instructions lines 124-126: medical expenses "if you itemize deductions on Schedule A") AND Schedule A has medical expenses (scheduleA:/allowableMedicalExpenses more than $0).
UNANSWERED: on that population this person's line 2 column (d) amount (../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) and the credit are Incomplete; everywhere else it is not asked and nothing is subtracted.
VALIDATION: a dollar amount, not less than $0; the netted amount never goes below $0.
FEEDS: subtracted from ../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount inside ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, which is line 2 column (d), and so line 3 and line 30. Schedule A itself does not change: the answer is dollars the filer kept in Schedule A line 1. Care expenses that are also medical expenses can be used "either way, but you can't use the same expenses to claim both a credit and a medical expense deduction" (Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 10), so the filer's Schedule A entry is taken as that choice and those dollars leave the credit. IRC 213(e) is the statute's one-use rule: an expense allowed as the credit is not treated as a medical expense.

Fact.Name: Qualifying Expense Amount for CDCC
Fact.Description:
Form 2441 line 2 column (d) for this qualifying person: the qualified expenses the filer both incurred AND paid in 2025 for this person's care, less any part a state social services agency reimbursed.
QUESTION TEXT: "How much did you pay in 2025 for care this person received in 2025? Don't include any amount a state social services agency paid you back."
HELP TEXT: Expenses a state social services agency reimburses aren't qualified expenses, so enter what you paid minus what the agency reimbursed (i2441 lines 73-74; Pub. 503 lines 679-682). Example (Pub. 503 lines 683-685): you paid $3,000 for this person's care and a state social services agency reimbursed you $2,000; enter $1,000. The amount you paid each care provider (Form 2441 line 1 column (e)) is asked separately and is NOT reduced by any reimbursement (i2441 lines 153-157, right column).
HELP TEXT, THE WORK-RELATED PART: "Enter only what you paid so that you (and your spouse, if filing jointly) could work or look for work. If a payment was partly for care that let you work and partly for something else, enter only the work-related part - you don't have to split it if only a small part was for something else. If you worked or looked for work for only part of the time the care covered, count only the care for that part: for example, $250 a month all year while you worked only 2 1/2 months is $625. If you work part-time, count care for the days you worked (a day with at least 1 hour of work is a work day) - unless the provider charges by the week or month whatever days you use, in which case the whole charge can count. Unpaid volunteer work is not work." (Pub. 503 lines 408-440 and 508-513; IRC 21(b)(2)(A).)
HELP TEXT, HOUSEHOLD SERVICES: "You can include what you paid for household services - a cook, maid, babysitter, housekeeper or cleaning person - if the services were at least partly for the care of this person. Don't include a chauffeur, bartender or gardener." (Pub. 503 lines 489-500, right column.)
HELP TEXT, THE 13TH BIRTHDAY (a child, not a disabled spouse or dependent): "If this child turned 13 during 2025, include only care for the part of the year before the 13th birthday. For example, $500 a month of after-school care for a child who turned 13 on May 1 counts $2,000, for January through April." A child who turned 13 during the year is a qualifying person only for the part of the year they were under age 13 (i2441 lines 64-66, left column; Pub. 503 Example 1, lines 792-796, right column). The graph receives one dollar figure per person and has no birthday split, so the restriction is carried by the question: the amount entered IS the pre-birthday amount, and ../cdccTurnedThirteenAfterJanFirst admits the child as a qualifying person for that part only.
HELP TEXT, A CHILD WHO TURNED 13 AND CANNOT CARE FOR THEMSELVES: "If this child turned 13 during 2025 and is physically or mentally unable to care for themselves, include care for the whole year, before and after the birthday." After the birthday the child is still a qualifying person as a dependent incapable of self-care who lived with you more than half the year (IRC 21(b)(1)(B)); care given outside your home after the birthday counts only if the child regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home (IRC 21(b)(2)(B)(ii)).
TIMING — the amount asked for is care INCURRED in 2025 and PAID in 2025. Three kinds of expense do not belong in it (Form 2441's own caution above line 2, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, pages 3-4): • care this person received in 2024 that you did not pay for until 2025. Enter those on the separate 2024-expenses-paid-in-2025 question (cdcc:/writableCdccPriorYearExpensesPaidInCurrentYear); they reach the credit through Worksheet A and Form 2441 line 9b, so entering them here as well claims the same dollars twice — once through line 3 and again through line 9b; • care received in 2025 that you will not pay for until 2026. Those may increase your 2026 credit instead; • care you prepaid in 2025 for care to be provided in 2026. Those can only be used to figure your 2026 credit.
NOT CARE — leave these out of the amount (i2441 lines 115-123; Pub. 503 lines 443-470): • an OVERNIGHT camp. No amount paid for services outside your household at a camp where this person stays overnight is a qualified expense (IRC 21(b)(2)(A), closing sentence). A DAY camp does count, even one that specializes in an activity such as computers or soccer; • schooling at the kindergarten level or above, summer school, and tutoring programs. Nursery school, preschool and similar programs BELOW the kindergarten level ARE care, and so is before- or after-school care of a child in kindergarten or a higher grade; • food, lodging, clothing, education and entertainment, unless the amount is incidental to the care and cannot be separated from the cost of the care.
BENEFITS — if you received dependent care benefits from an employer's plan, don't include care that was paid for with the benefits that were EXCLUDED FROM YOUR INCOME (Form 2441 line 28, cdcc:/cdccSumOfDeductibleAndExcludedBenefitsAmount). Care you paid for with benefits that were TAXABLE to you (Form 2441 line 26) does count — those dollars are wages. The total you leave out across all of the persons on this return should not exceed line 28. This is what Form 2441 line 30 means by "Don't include in column (d) any benefits shown on line 28 above." (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 2; 2025 Instructions for Form 2441, Column (d), "If you completed Part III, don't include in column (d) any benefits shown on line 28.", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3). THE GRAPH DOES NOT ASK A SECOND TIME AND DOES NOT SUBTRACT LINE 28 FOR YOU: the total qualified expenses question (Form 2441 line 16, cdcc:/writableCdccTotalQualifiedDependentCareExpenses) is the GROSS figure that DOES include employer-covered care, and this question is the net one. Line 16 also counts expenses you INCURRED in 2025 whenever paid ("It doesn't matter when the expenses were paid", i2441 lines 375-377), so line 16 minus line 28 is not this amount and cannot be used to derive it.
ASKED WHEN: this person is a qualifying person for the credit and ../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses is true (the person had dependent care expenses paid to a qualified provider).
UNANSWERED: stays unanswered; ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount and the credit are Incomplete, never a default.
VALIDATION: a dollar amount.
FEEDS: ../cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, which is line 2 column (d); its sum with the other qualifying persons' amounts is line 3 before the dollar limit, and line 30 on a Part III return.

Fact.Name: Some of this person's care was provided outside your home
Fact.Description:
Whether any part of the care COVERED BY THE AMOUNT ENTERED for this person (../writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, Form 2441 column (d)) was provided OUTSIDE the taxpayer's household.
QUESTION TEXT: "Was any of the care included in the amount you entered for this person provided somewhere other than your home?"
SCOPED TO THE AMOUNT, DELIBERATELY. An earlier wording asked about the person's care in the abstract ("Was any of this person's care provided somewhere other than your home?"), and nothing the filer could honestly do would then clear cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest: that refusal reads no dollar, so reducing the amount to the in-home part — the remedy the knockout's own Description promised — changed none of the flag's conjuncts, and the only exit left was to answer this question falsely. Scoped to the amount, the promised remedy works as written: a filer who leaves the out-of-home dollars out of column (d) answers No truthfully, the 8-hour question below is never reached, and the refusal clears.
HELP TEXT: Care at a daycare centre, a day camp, a relative's house or anywhere else that is not your home is care provided outside your home. Care given in your home by a babysitter, nanny or housekeeper is not. Answer about the amount you just entered, not about the person's whole year. Why it is asked: for a person who is NOT your dependent child under 13, care outside your home counts toward the credit only if that person regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home ("You can include the cost of care provided outside your home for your dependent under age 13, or any other qualifying person who regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 2; Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 7). If this person does not regularly spend 8 hours a day in your home, go back and enter only what you paid for care given IN your home — then the answer here is No.
FOR A CHILD WHO TURNED 13 DURING THE YEAR AND CANNOT CARE FOR THEMSELVES the question is about the care after the 13th birthday only: "Was any of the care after this child's 13th birthday that is included in the amount you entered provided somewhere other than your home?" Care before the birthday was care of a child under 13 and counts wherever it was given.
ASKED WHEN: this person is a qualifying person for the credit (../cdccQualifyingPerson) who is NOT a paragraph (1)(A) individual — that is, ../age is 13 or more AND ../cdccTurnedThirteenAfterJanFirst is false, OR the person turned 13 during the year and is unable to care for themselves (../unableToCareForSelf), OR the person is under 13 but is not a dependent (neither ../eligibleDependent nor the custodial parent's released child) and qualifies only as a person incapable of self-care — AND ../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses is true. A dependent under 13 is exempt from the 8-hour test by IRC 21(b)(2)(B)(i) and is never asked, even if they are also unable to care for themselves. The expenses conjunct is now IN ../cdccFailsOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest's own All, IsComplete-guarded — a person with no qualifying expenses contributes $0 to the credit and is never refused over where their care happened.
UNANSWERED: nothing refuses and nothing is Incomplete — cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest is IsComplete-first and resolves false, exactly as cdcc:/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider does for its own attestation (ruling 6: a question the filer never reached never refuses). The application must carry this as a required screen on the person's care card.
VALIDATION: Boolean, Yes / No.
FEEDS: ../cdccFailsOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest, and through it cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest.

Fact.Name: This person regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home
Fact.Description:
Whether this qualifying person regularly spends at least 8 hours EACH DAY in the taxpayer's household — IRC 21(b)(2)(B)(ii)'s test for counting care given outside the home.
QUESTION TEXT: "Does this person regularly spend at least 8 hours a day in your home?"
HELP TEXT: This is about the person, not about the care. It is the test that decides whether the care you paid for outside your home counts toward the credit at all ("any other qualifying person who regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in your home", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 2; Pub. 503, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 7). If the answer is No, go back and take the amounts you paid for care given outside your home out of this person's care expenses — only care given IN your home counts for them — and the previous question, which asks about the amount you entered, then becomes a truthful No.
ASKED WHEN: ../writableCdccCareProvidedOutsideHousehold is true. Not asked otherwise: the test only decides whether OUT-OF-HOME care can be counted.
UNANSWERED: nothing refuses and nothing is Incomplete — see ../writableCdccCareProvidedOutsideHousehold's UNANSWERED note; the refusal is IsComplete-first.
VALIDATION: Boolean, Yes / No.
FEEDS: ../cdccFailsOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest, and through it cdcc:/knockoutCdccOutsideHouseholdEightHourTest.

Fact.Name: Out-of-home care for a person who fails the 8-hour test
Fact.Description:
This qualifying person is not a child under 13, some of their care was given outside the taxpayer's home, and they do not regularly spend at least 8 hours a day in that home — so IRC 21(b)(2)(B) does not let the out-of-home part of their expenses be taken into account. Complete-safe: false whenever either attestation is unanswered.
THE EXPENSES CONJUNCT. ../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses is read here, IsComplete-guarded like its siblings, so a person the filer claims no care expenses for is never refused over where their care happened: their column (d) contribution is $0 and no disallowed dollar can reach the credit through them. Without the guard the unanswered-expense path would go Incomplete rather than false, which is the failure class this fact's other IsComplete pairs exist to prevent. Note the location attestation is scoped to the AMOUNT ENTERED, not to the person's care in the abstract — that is what makes this refusal correctable, see ../writableCdccCareProvidedOutsideHousehold's own Description.
THE UNDER-13 EXCLUSION IS A (1)(A) TEST: A DEPENDENT UNDER 13, NOT AN INCAPACITY TEST. IRC 21(b)(2)(B)(i) exempts every paragraph (1)(A) qualifying individual — a dependent who has not attained age 13 — from the 8-hour condition, whether or not that child is also unable to care for themselves. The age leg is the age test ../cdccQualifyingPerson's own qualifying-child arm applies (age under 13, or ../cdccTurnedThirteenAfterJanFirst, which keeps a child who turned 13 during the year inside paragraph (1)(A) for the part of the year they were under it). The dependent leg is ../eligibleDependent, or the custodial parent's released child that IRC 21(e)(5) treats as a (1)(A) individual. An under-13 person who is a qualifying person only through the third route of ../cdccNonDependentQualifyingPerson (not a dependent - for example because the filer can be claimed by someone else - but incapable of self-care) is a (1)(B) individual, and the 8-hour test applies to their out-of-home care.
A CHILD WHO TURNED 13 DURING THE YEAR AND CANNOT CARE FOR THEMSELVES is a (1)(A) individual only until the 13th birthday and a (1)(B) individual after it (IRC 21(b)(1)(B)), so the amount entered for that child can include care after the birthday, and out-of-home care after the birthday counts only if the child regularly spends at least 8 hours a day in the home. Such a child is therefore not exempt here: the outside-household question is asked about care after the 13th birthday (see ../writableCdccCareProvidedOutsideHousehold).
