Fact.Name: Residency duration
Fact.Description:
The portion of 2025 the person lived with the taxpayer, as one of four answers. It is the more-than-half-of-the-year residency line of IRC 152(c)(1)(B), IRC 21(b)(1)(B) and (C), and IRC 2(b)(1)(A), in the shape the interview asks it.
QUESTION TEXT: "How much of 2025 did this person live with you?"
OPTIONS AND THEIR LABELS. The line is MORE THAN HALF OF 2025, not a count of calendar months: a person who lived with you six months and ten days lived with you more than half of 2025 and answers the second option. - allYear: "All year" - sevenToElevenMonths: "More than half of 2025 but not all year" - sixMonths: "Six months, but not more than half of 2025" - lessThanSixMonths: "Less than six months" This is the printed convention of Schedule EIC line 6, "If the child lived with you for more than half of 2025 but less than 7 months, enter '7'" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sei.pdf, page 1). Only the first two options pass the residency test.
HELP TEXT, AND IT IS PART OF THE QUESTION, NOT A FOOTNOTE. Time either of them was away on a TEMPORARY ABSENCE for a special circumstance COUNTS as time the person lived with the taxpayer. The 2025 Form 1040 instructions name the circumstances: "Temporary absences by you or the other person for special circumstances, such as school, vacation, business, medical care, military service, or detention in a juvenile facility, count as time the person lived with you." Publication 501 lists the same set as illness, education, business, vacation, military service and detention in a juvenile facility. A filer who subtracts a semester at university, a hospital stay or a deployment answers this question wrongly and loses a dependency the statute grants, so the application must put this rule ON the screen rather than behind a help link.
WHAT IS NOT IN THIS ANSWER. A child born or died in 2025 is handled by ../bornOrDiedResidencyException, not by a bucket, because such a child cannot truthfully pick one.
UNANSWERED: stays unanswered; the residency test is Incomplete rather than defaulted, and nothing downstream reads a favourable guess.
STATE SYSTEMS: this answer is exported to state systems, and the four option names above are its vocabulary there.

Fact.Name: Residency test
Fact.Description: Did the dependent live with you for more than half the year? Used for dependents other than QSS.

Fact.Name: Born or died during the tax year
Fact.Description:
The person was born in the tax year OR died in the tax year - the population Publication 501's "Death or birth of child" exception and the Form 1040 instructions' "Exception to time lived with you" are written about.
SCOPED TO THE PRINTED RULE, DELIBERATELY WIDER THAN ../bornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin. The exception says "born OR died", so a child born in 2024 who died in 2025, and a child born in 2025 who is alive at year end, both get it. Gating it on ../bornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin (born AND died AND no TIN) would have been the narrower population the documentation route needs, and would have left the printed rule half-built for everyone else.
Exported downstream because it is the ASKED-WHEN gate for ../writableBornOrDiedLivedWithTpMostOfLife.

Fact.Name: Lived with the taxpayer for most of the time they were alive
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to the born-or-died residency exception: was this home the person's home for more than half the time they were alive during the tax year?
WHY IT CANNOT BE INFERRED. ../residencyDuration asks "What portion of the YEAR did the dependent live with you?" and its four options are allYear / sevenToElevenMonths / sixMonths / lessThanSixMonths. A child alive for 40 days truthfully answers lessThanSixMonths, and no arithmetic over the year turns that into the exception's answer, which is measured against the part of the year the person was ALIVE, not against the year. It is a different question and it needs its own answer.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION - the application implements this without opening an IRS document.
SCREEN NAME (proposed): BornOrDiedLivedWithYou, in the Dependents section, immediately after the ../residencyDuration screen for this person.
QUESTION TEXT, as asked, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "Was your home {name}'s home for more than half of the time {name} was alive in 2025?"
HELP TEXT, paraphrasing the governing instruction: "Because {name} was born or died in 2025, the usual "more than half the year" test is measured differently: {name} counts as having lived with you for more than half of 2025 if your home was {name}'s home for more than half of the time {name} was alive during the year. A required hospital stay right after birth still counts as time spent with you. Answer Yes if that is true." Sources: Publication 501, Death or birth of child - "A child who was born or died during the year is treated as having lived with you more than half the year if your home was the child's home more than half the time the child was alive during the year. The same is true if the child lived with you more than half the year except for any required hospital stay following birth" - https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p501.pdf, page 13 (three-column extraction, so the sentence runs down alternating lines); and the 2025 Instructions for Form 1040, Exception to time lived with you - https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 21, LEFT column (the born-or-died sentence at 1211-1215; the adopted-or-placed limb at 1215-1222).
ASKED WHEN: ../bornOrDiedInTaxYear is Complete true for this person. Ask it ONCE PER PERSON. It is worth asking even when ../residencyDuration is already allYear or sevenToElevenMonths - the answer is then redundant, not wrong - but the application may skip it in that case, because the arm it feeds is an Any beside the ordinary test and cannot take anything away.
UNANSWERED POSTURE, and why. Unanswered means NO for the residency test itself: ../bornOrDiedResidencyException gates this writable on its own IsComplete, so an unanswered screen resolves Complete false and ../residencyTest reads exactly as it read before this unit - which is what keeps every committed scenario byte-identical.
AND UNANSWERED IS ALSO NOT THE SAME AS "NO" ANYWHERE IT MATTERS (re-review B1-R). ../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin carries IsComplete of THIS writable as a conjunct, so for a born-and-died child an unasked screen keeps /knockoutPersonBornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin refusing rather than letting the return file with the claim silently denied. Answered No is different: the filer told us the child did not live with them for most of their life, the child correctly fails the residency test, the claim is correctly denied and NO knockout fires. VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, labels "Yes" / "No", no default selection, answer required to leave the screen. No Min/Max.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../bornOrDiedResidencyException -> ../residencyTest -> ../qualifyingChild, and from there the dependency claim, the CTC/ODC legs and the head-of-household qualifying-person chain. It ALSO reaches ../livedWithTpInUsMostOfYear, which reads ../residencyTest directly - but there it is a VALUE NO-OP, because that fact's other leg reads this exception too (its months Any carries ../bornOrDiedResidencyException as an arm, because a child alive for part of one year cannot answer the months bucket). It also widens Form 8862 Part III line 14's "lived with you more than half the year OR met an exception described in the instructions" box, which is correct: the exception is one of the exceptions that box is about.
THE OTHER LIMBS OF THE PRINTED RULE live in their own facts: the adopted-or-placed limb ("more than half the time since the person was adopted or placed with you in 2025") is ../adoptedOrPlacedResidencyException, and i1040gi's stricter "Any other person" limb for a qualifying RELATIVE (the home was the person's home for the ENTIRE time they were alive) is ../qssBornOrDiedResidencyException, read by ../memberOfHouseholdTest.

Fact.Name: The born-or-died residency exception is met
Fact.Description:
The person was born or died in the tax year AND the taxpayer answered that this home was the person's home for more than half the time they were alive. That is the whole of the printed exception, and it is the arm ../residencyTest reads beside its ordinary test.
COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION, which is what keeps ../residencyTest's completeness profile identical to what it was without the exception: both legs are gated on their own IsComplete, so an unanswered date of birth, an unanswered deceased flag or an unanswered exception answer all resolve Complete false rather than Incomplete. ../residencyTest is read bare in a dozen places and is mef-exported; turning it Incomplete anywhere would have been a corpus-wide regression.

Fact.Name: Presumed by law enforcement to have been kidnapped by someone outside both families
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to the head question of the IRC 152(f)(6) missing-children rule: is this child "presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who is not a member of the family of such child or the taxpayer"?
THE NON-FAMILY-MEMBER QUALIFIER IS PART OF THE QUESTION, NOT A FOOTNOTE. The statute grants the treatment only where the presumed kidnapper is outside BOTH families - the child's and the taxpayer's. A child taken by an estranged parent, a grandparent or a sibling is outside the rule, however genuine the abduction, and a screen that asks only "was your child kidnapped?" collects a Yes the statute does not support.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION - the application implements this without opening an IRS document.
SCREEN NAME (proposed): KidnappedChild, in the Dependents section, offered after the ../residencyDuration screen for this person.
QUESTION TEXT, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "Do law enforcement authorities presume that {name} was kidnapped by someone who is not a member of your family or {name}'s family?"
HELP TEXT: a child who meets this rule is treated as having lived with you for the whole period of the kidnapping, so the usual "more than half the year" test does not deny the claim. The rule applies only where the presumed kidnapper is not a member of your family or the child's family. Sources: IRC 152(f)(6)(A)(i), and Publication 596, "Kidnapped child - The child must be presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn't a member of your family or the child's family."
ASKED WHEN: this person is being tested as a qualifying child and ../residencyDuration is lessThanSixMonths, or the EIC months bucket cannot be answered. It is the HEAD question of a three-question group; the other two are asked only if this one is answered Yes.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: unanswered means NO for the exception, and that is the ADVERSE direction, not a favourable default - the ordinary residency test then decides, exactly as it did before this fact existed. Every committed return leaves this unanswered, so none of them moves. Answered YES is different: the return is then CLAIMING the exception, and the two follow-ups become conditions of allowance whose absence is a genuine Incomplete rather than a silent denial.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection, no Min/Max.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../kidnappedChildResidencyException -> ../residencyTest and ../livedWithTpInUsMostOfYear, and through the latter the EIC qualifying-child chain and the printed Schedule EIC line 6 entry, which prints "KC" instead of a numeral.

Fact.Name: Same principal place of abode for more than half the part of the kidnapping year before the kidnapping
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to IRC 152(f)(6)(A)(ii): in the taxable year the kidnapping occurred, did this child have the same principal place of abode as the taxpayer for more than one-half of the portion of that year BEFORE the date of the kidnapping?
IT IS AN ATTESTATION AND IT CANNOT BE DERIVED. The measurement is against a part of a possibly PRIOR year - the year the kidnapping occurred, which may be 2023 or 2019 - and the graph holds nothing about a prior year's living arrangements. Even where the kidnapping happened in 2025, the only figures this dictionary has are ../residencyDuration, whose three buckets are measured against the whole year, and ../monthsLivedWithTPInUS, which floors at six months; neither can express "more than half of the part of the year before the date of the kidnapping". So this is asked, not computed, and the date of the kidnapping is not collected at all.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION. SCREEN NAME (proposed): KidnappedChildAbode, asked ONLY when ../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember is Yes and ../writableKidnappedChildNotReturnedByEndOfTaxYear is Yes.
QUESTION TEXT, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "In the year {name} was kidnapped, did {name} live in your home for more than half of the part of that year before the kidnapping happened?"
HELP TEXT: this looks at the year the kidnapping happened, which may be an earlier year than 2025, and only at the part of that year BEFORE the kidnapping. A child returned during 2025 is measured instead by the part of 2025 after the return (../writableKidnappedChildLivedWithTpMostOfYearAfterReturn).
UNANSWERED POSTURE, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT COMPLETE-SAFE. Once ../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember is Yes the return is CLAIMING this exception, and an unanswered condition of allowance on a claiming return resolves genuine Incomplete - up through ../kidnappedChildResidencyException, ../residencyTest and the credit chain to flow:/flowIncomplete, which blocks submission. It is never a silent false: a complete-safe false here would deny a child the statute grants, on a return that has told us the child was kidnapped.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection, required once the head question is Yes.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../kidnappedChildResidencyException.

Fact.Name: No determination that the kidnapped child is dead was made before the tax year began
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to the first limb of the IRC 152(f)(6)(D) termination rule: was there NO determination that this child is dead before 1 January 2025?
WHY THE QUESTION IS PHRASED THAT WAY, AND WHY THE YEAR MATTERS. (D) ends the treatment "as of the first taxable year of the taxpayer beginning after the calendar year in which there is a determination that the child is dead". So a determination made during 2024 ends the treatment for TY2025, and a determination made during 2025 does NOT - the treatment still covers 2025 and ends with 2026. The question therefore asks about determinations made BEFORE the tax year began, not about determinations at all.
AN ATTESTATION RATHER THAN A YEAR INTAKE, and the choice is recorded here. A year intake ("in what year was a determination made?") would carry more information and would let a future unit compute the termination for any tax year. It was not built because the answer this dictionary needs for TY2025 is a single Boolean, and a year intake would need its own unanswered posture, its own bound and its own screen for a population of returns that is very close to empty. A successor that generalises the rule across tax years should replace this fact with the year.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION. SCREEN NAME (proposed): KidnappedChildStillMissing, asked ONLY when ../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember is Yes.
QUESTION TEXT, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "Before 1 January 2025, had there been any determination that {name} is dead?" - and the fact stores the NEGATION, so a No on that screen is a Yes here. The application may instead ask it positively: "As of 1 January 2025, was {name} still missing, with no determination that {name} is dead?"
HELP TEXT: the special treatment for a kidnapped child ends with the tax year AFTER the calendar year in which there is a determination that the child is dead, or, if earlier, the year the child would have reached age 18. The age half is computed from the date of birth already on this return and is not asked.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: genuine Incomplete once the head question is Yes, for the same reason as ../writableKidnappedChildAbodeBeforeKidnapping - it is a condition of allowance on a claiming return, never a silent false.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection, required once the head question is Yes.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../kidnappedChildResidencyException.

Fact.Name: The kidnapped-child treatment has not been ended for this tax year by the age-18 limb
Fact.Description:
The age half of the IRC 152(f)(6)(D) termination rule, derived rather than asked: the treatment ends as of the first taxable year beginning after the calendar year in which the child would have attained age 18, so it still covers TY2025 exactly when the child would attain 18 in calendar 2025 or later.
THE BOUND, ON THE DAY-BEFORE-THE-BIRTHDAY CONVENTION. A person attains an age on the day before the anniversary of their birth, the convention the Form 1040 instructions print for the same statute's age words ("A child born on January 1, 2008, is considered to be age 18 at the end of 2025"). ../ageCalculatedDayBeforeDOB is the tax year minus the year of the day before the birthday, so a child who attains 18 during calendar 2025 (born 2007-01-02 through 2008-01-01) has it 18 and is still covered, and a child born on or before 2007-01-01 attained 18 during calendar 2024 or earlier, has it 19 or more, and for that child the first taxable year beginning after the year of attaining 18 is TY2025 itself, so the treatment has ended. The bound is therefore ../ageCalculatedDayBeforeDOB at most 18. ../youngerThanEighteenAtEndOfYear is one year too strict for this rule and is not reused.
INCOMPLETE WHEN THE DATE OF BIRTH IS. ../ageCalculatedDayBeforeDOB is Incomplete on an unanswered or out-of-bound date of birth, so this fact is too, and on a return claiming the exception that Incomplete is the correct refusal rather than a guess about the child's age.

Fact.Name: The IRC 152(f)(6) kidnapped-child residency exception is met
Fact.Description:
The whole of the IRC 152(f)(6) missing-children rule as this dictionary can state it: a child presumed by law enforcement to have been kidnapped by someone outside both families, who had the taxpayer's principal place of abode for more than half of the part of the kidnapping year before the kidnapping, is treated as meeting the section 152(c)(1)(B) residency requirement for every taxable year ending during the period the child is kidnapped - so the child must still be missing when TY2025 ends, unless the child was returned during 2025 and meets Publication 596's return-year limb - and the treatment has not yet been ended for TY2025 by either limb of (D).
SOLELY FOR FOUR PURPOSES. (f)(6)(A) grants the treatment "solely for the purposes referred to in subparagraph (B)": the section 151(c) dependency, the section 24 child tax credit and credit for other dependents, head-of-household or surviving-spouse status under section 2, and the section 32 earned income credit. So this fact is NOT an arm of ../residencyTest, which the section 21 dependent-care facts also read. It reaches ../residencyTestWithKidnappedChildTreatment (read by ../qualifyingChild), ../livedWithTpInUsMostOfYear, ../qssPersonResidencyTest and the Schedule EIC line 6 print, and nothing else.
THE POSTURE IS NOT ../bornOrDiedResidencyException'S, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS DELIBERATE. That fact is complete-safe false in every unanswered state, because its follow-up is a single question whose absence leaves the ordinary test to decide. Here the head question splits the population in two. While ../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember is unanswered or answered No, this fact is Complete FALSE - the ordinary months and residency tests decide, which is the adverse direction and not a favourable default, and every committed return in the corpus is in that state. The moment it is answered YES the return is CLAIMING the exception, and the three attestations, the age conjunct AND the relationship conjunct (../isChildWithinMeaningOf152f1: this person must be a "child of the taxpayer" under 152(f)(1), not merely the wider relationshipCategoryIsChild category) become conditions of allowance: they are read BARE, with no IsComplete wrapper and with no catch-all arm after the two cases, so an unanswered follow-up resolves genuine Incomplete on this fact, on ../residencyTest, on ../livedWithTpInUsMostOfYear and up the chain to flow:/flowIncomplete. An IsComplete conjunct would be a complete-safe wrapper by another name and would silently deny a child the statute grants.
THE RETURN-YEAR LIMB. Publication 596 measures the abode condition against the part of the year before the kidnapping OR the part following the child's return. A child still missing on 31 December 2025 takes the first (../writableKidnappedChildAbodeBeforeKidnapping); a child returned during 2025 takes the second (../writableKidnappedChildLivedWithTpMostOfYearAfterReturn), read complete-safe, so an unanswered after-return question leaves the ordinary tests to decide.
THE QUALIFYING-RELATIVE TWIN is ../kidnappedChildQualifyingRelativeTreatment (IRC 152(f)(6)(C)), read by ../qualifyingRelative. The MeF element for a Schedule EIC line 6 "KC" entry is not in this repo's sources, so the exception feeds the printed entry only.

Fact.Name: The qualifying-child residency test, with the IRC 152(f)(6) kidnapped-child treatment
Fact.Description:
The section 152(c)(1)(B) residency test as it applies for the four purposes IRC 152(f)(6)(B) lists - the section 151(c) dependency, the section 24 child tax credit and credit for other dependents, head-of-household or surviving-spouse status under section 2, and the section 32 earned income credit: ../residencyTest, or the kidnapped- child treatment ../kidnappedChildResidencyException.
WHY IT IS A SEPARATE FACT. ../residencyTest is also read by the section 21 dependent-care facts, and (f)(6)(A) grants the treatment "solely" for the purposes in (B), which do not include section 21. So the plain test keeps its meaning for section 21, and this fact is what the covered purposes read: ../qualifyingChild and ../livedWithTpInUsMostOfYear.
COMPLETENESS. The exception is Complete false whenever its head question is unanswered or No, so this fact has exactly ../residencyTest's value and completeness on every such return. It is Incomplete only where a return claims the exception and leaves a condition of allowance blank, which is the intended refusal.

Fact.Name: The kidnapped child was still missing, not yet returned, at the end of the tax year
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to the end of the IRC 152(f)(6) treatment that the other questions do not reach: was this child still missing - not yet returned - on 31 December 2025?
WHY IT IS ASKED. (f)(6)(A) applies "for all taxable years ending during the period that the child is kidnapped", and Publication 596 prints it as "This treatment applies for all years until the child is returned." TY2025 ends on 31 December 2025, so it is covered only if the child was still missing then. Neither the head question nor the two (D) questions asks this: a child kidnapped in 2020 and returned in 2021, still under 18 with no determination of death, answers every other question exactly like a child still missing.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION. SCREEN NAME (proposed): KidnappedChildStillMissing, asked ONLY when ../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember is Yes.
QUESTION TEXT, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "On 31 December 2025, was {name} still missing - not yet returned to you?"
HELP TEXT: the special treatment for a kidnapped child applies for every year that ends while the child is missing. If {name} was returned at any time before the end of 2025, answer No; the next question then asks how long {name} lived with you after coming back.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: genuine Incomplete once the head question is Yes. It is a condition of allowance on a claiming return, so its absence stops the return rather than qualifying the child silently. It also decides which measuring period applies: Yes reads ../writableKidnappedChildAbodeBeforeKidnapping, No reads ../writableKidnappedChildLivedWithTpMostOfYearAfterReturn.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection, required once the head question is Yes.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../kidnappedChildResidencyException.

Fact.Name: A kidnapped child returned in 2025 lived with the taxpayer for more than half of the rest of the year
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer, for a kidnapped child who was returned during 2025: did this child live with the taxpayer for more than half of the part of 2025 that followed the child's return?
WHY IT IS ASKED. Publication 596 states the kidnapped-child treatment with two measuring periods: "A kidnapped child is treated as living with you for more than half of the year if the child lived with you for more than half the part of the year before the date of the kidnapping or following the date of the child's return." A child still missing at the end of 2025 is measured by the first (../writableKidnappedChildAbodeBeforeKidnapping). A child returned during 2025 is measured by the second, and this is that question.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION. SCREEN NAME (proposed): KidnappedChildAfterReturn, asked ONLY when ../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember is Yes and ../writableKidnappedChildNotReturnedByEndOfTaxYear is No.
QUESTION TEXT, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "After {name} was returned in 2025, did {name} live with you for more than half of the rest of 2025?"
HELP TEXT: count from the day {name} came back to 31 December 2025. If {name} lived with you for more than half of that time, answer Yes. Time away on a temporary absence, such as school or a hospital stay, counts as time living with you.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: treated as No, the adverse direction: the kidnapped-child treatment is not applied and the usual rule about how long {name} lived with you decides, as it did before this question existed.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../kidnappedChildResidencyException.

Fact.Name: The kidnapped child was the taxpayer's qualifying relative for the part of the year before the kidnapping
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to IRC 152(f)(6)(C)(ii): leaving the kidnapping aside, was this child the taxpayer's qualifying relative for the part of the kidnapping year before the date of the kidnapping? That is, did the taxpayer provide more than half of the child's support for that part of the year, was the child's gross income under the limit, and was the child not anyone's qualifying child?
WHY IT IS ASKED. Section 152(f)(6)(C) treats such a child as the taxpayer's qualifying relative "for all taxable years ending during the period that the child is kidnapped". It is the twin of the qualifying-child treatment and it reaches the child the qualifying-child treatment does not: one who did not share the taxpayer's home before the kidnapping, but whom the taxpayer supported. The measurement is against a part of a possibly earlier year, so it is an attestation, not a computation.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION. SCREEN NAME (proposed): KidnappedChildQualifyingRelative, asked ONLY when ../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember is Yes and this person is not a qualifying child of the taxpayer (../qualifyingChild false).
QUESTION TEXT, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "For the part of the year {name} was kidnapped, before the kidnapping, did you provide more than half of {name}'s support, with {name}'s gross income under the limit and {name} not anyone's qualifying child?"
HELP TEXT: this looks at the year the kidnapping happened, which may be an earlier year than 2025, and only at the part of that year before the kidnapping. If it was true then, the law treats {name} as your qualifying relative for every year that ends while {name} is still missing, until the year after a determination that {name} is dead or the year {name} would have turned 18.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: treated as No, the adverse direction: the ordinary qualifying-relative tests decide, as they did before this question existed.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../kidnappedChildQualifyingRelativeTreatment.

Fact.Name: The IRC 152(f)(6)(C) kidnapped-child qualifying-relative treatment applies
Fact.Description:
IRC 152(f)(6)(C): a child of the taxpayer, presumed by law enforcement to have been kidnapped by someone outside both families, who was the taxpayer's qualifying relative for the part of the kidnapping year before the kidnapping, is treated as the taxpayer's qualifying relative for every taxable year ending while the child is kidnapped, until (D) ends the treatment.
FOR EVERY PURPOSE OF SECTION 152. (A) is limited to four purposes; (C) applies "for purposes of this section", so the child is a qualifying relative for the dependency and everything that follows from it, including the credit for other dependents.
POSTURE. Complete FALSE unless the head question (../writableKidnappedByNonFamilyMember) and ../writableKidnappedChildWasQualifyingRelativeBeforeKidnapping are both answered Yes, so no return that has not claimed the treatment moves. Once both are Yes the return is claiming it, and the remaining conditions of allowance - the 152(f)(1) child relationship, still missing on 31 December 2025, no determination of death before 2025, and the (D) age bound - are read bare, so an unanswered one is Incomplete rather than a silent denial or a silent grant.

Fact.Name: Home was the person's home for the entire time they were alive (born-or-died exception, qualifying surviving spouse and member of household)
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to the qualifying-surviving-spouse-specific born-or-died exception: was this home the person's home for the ENTIRE time they were alive during the tax year (not merely more than half)? Qualifying surviving spouse asks a STRICTER version of the ordinary born-or-died exception ../writableBornOrDiedLivedWithTpMostOfLife answers: Publication 501 and the Form 1040 instructions give the QSS person test its own words, "the entire part of the year the child was alive" / "the entire time the child was alive", where the ordinary dependency/HOH exception reads "more than half the time." The two are NOT the same question, and a Yes to the ordinary (more-than-half) exception does not answer this one: a home that was the child's home for, say, two of the three months a child born in October was alive answers the ordinary exception Yes and this one No.
ASKED WHEN: ../bornOrDiedInTaxYear is Complete true for this person and qualifying surviving spouse is otherwise reachable (the application's screen-flow decision; there is no fact-graph gate narrower than the born-or-died population itself, matching the ordinary born-or-died writable's own shape).
UNANSWERED POSTURE: Complete-safe false. ../qssBornOrDiedResidencyException gates this writable on its own IsComplete, so an unanswered screen resolves Complete false and ../qssPersonResidencyTest reads exactly as it read before this fact existed, the adverse (non-favorable) direction, not exploitable.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No, answer required to leave the screen.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../qssBornOrDiedResidencyException -> ../qssPersonResidencyTest -> ../qssQualifyingPerson -> filingStatus:/eligibleForQss.
A SECOND READER, THE SAME QUESTION. The member-of-household limb of the qualifying-relative relationship test (../memberOfHouseholdTest) uses the same entire-time standard for a person born or died during the year: the Form 1040 instructions say "any other person" is treated as having lived with the taxpayer all year if the taxpayer's home was the person's home for the entire time the person was alive, and Publication 501 says a person who died but lived with the taxpayer until death, or a child born during the year who lived with the taxpayer for the rest of the year, meets that test. So ../memberOfHouseholdTest reads ../qssBornOrDiedResidencyException too, and this question is also ASKED WHEN this person is not related to the taxpayer in one of the listed ways (dependentsRelationship:../qrRelationshipTest is false) and ../bornOrDiedInTaxYear is true, whether or not qualifying surviving spouse is reachable. It is one question, asked once per person, whichever reader needs it.
THE COMPANION LIMB: the adopted-or-placed-for-adoption half of the same printed rule ("for the entire time since this child was adopted or placed with you") is its own question, ../writableAdoptedOrPlacedQssLivedWithTpEntireTimeSincePlacement, gated on ../writableAdoptedOrPlacedForAdoptionDate.

Fact.Name: The entire-time born-or-died residency exception is met
Fact.Description:
The person was born or died in the tax year AND the taxpayer answered that this home was the person's home for the ENTIRE time they were alive, the qualifying-surviving-spouse-specific reading of the born-or-died exception, stricter than ../bornOrDiedResidencyException's more-than-half standard. Read by ../qssPersonResidencyTest and by ../memberOfHouseholdTest, whose born-or-died arm is the same entire-time standard.
COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION, matching ../bornOrDiedResidencyException's own shape: both legs are gated on their own IsComplete, so an unanswered date of birth, deceased flag or exception answer resolves Complete false rather than Incomplete.

Fact.Name: Date this person was adopted by you, or placed with you for legal adoption by you
Fact.Description:
The date the taxpayer adopted this person or, if earlier, the date the person was lawfully placed with the taxpayer for legal adoption by the taxpayer, or, for an eligible foster child, the date the child was placed with the taxpayer. It is the intake the adopted-or-placed exception to the time-lived-with-you rule is written about, and it lets that exception be tested against the tax year: the exception applies only to a child adopted or placed in the tax year.
ASKED WHEN: this person is the taxpayer's child by adoption, was placed with the taxpayer for adoption, or is an eligible foster child placed with the taxpayer, and the ordinary answer to how long the person lived with the taxpayer is less than the whole year. The foster placement is asked here because the Form 1040 instructions and Publications 501 and 596 print the same exception for "an eligible foster child placed with you during 2025"; it cannot reach the qualifying surviving spouse test, whose person test (../qssQualifyingPerson) admits only a son, daughter or stepchild, nor the adopted-child citizenship exception, which reads ../childIsAdopted.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: no default. Every reader gates on its IsComplete, so an unanswered date resolves the adopted-or-placed exception Complete false, which is how every return resolved before this intake existed.
VALIDATION: a calendar date on or before the last day of the tax year.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../adoptedOrPlacedForAdoptionInTaxYear -> ../qssAdoptedOrPlacedResidencyException (the entire-time limb: ../qssPersonResidencyTest, ../adoptedChildException) and ../adoptedOrPlacedResidencyException (the more-than-half limb: ../residencyTest and ../livedWithTpInUsMostOfYear).

Fact.Name: QSS: home was the child's home for the entire time since the adoption or placement
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to the qualifying-surviving-spouse adopted-or-placed exception: was the taxpayer's main home this child's main home for the ENTIRE time since the child was adopted by, or placed for legal adoption with, the taxpayer during the tax year? A Yes treats the child as having lived with the taxpayer for all of the year for the qualifying surviving spouse person test.
A STRICTER QUESTION THAN THE DEPENDENCY ONE. The ordinary dependency and head-of-household exception asks whether the home was the child's home for MORE THAN HALF the time since the adoption or placement. Qualifying surviving spouse asks for the entire time. A Yes to the more-than-half question does not answer this one: a child placed in March who spent May with a relative answers that question Yes and this one No.
ASKED WHEN: ../adoptedOrPlacedForAdoptionInTaxYear is Complete true for this person and either qualifying surviving spouse is otherwise reachable, or the child is an adopted or placed child who is not a U.S. citizen, U.S. national or U.S. resident (the citizenship exception, ../adoptedChildException, asks the same entire-time question: Publication 501's "lived with you for the rest of the year after placement"). The name keeps its Qss infix from the first reader; the question is the same for both.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: Complete-safe false. ../qssAdoptedOrPlacedResidencyException gates this writable on its own IsComplete, so an unanswered screen resolves Complete false and ../qssPersonResidencyTest reads exactly as it read before this fact existed, the adverse direction.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No, answer required to leave the screen.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../qssAdoptedOrPlacedResidencyException -> ../qssPersonResidencyTest -> ../qssQualifyingPerson -> filingStatus:/eligibleForQss, and ../adoptedChildException -> ../citizenOrResidentTest; a Yes also satisfies the looser more-than-half question read by ../adoptedOrPlacedResidencyException.

Fact.Name: Adopted or placed for legal adoption during the tax year
Fact.Description: True when ../writableAdoptedOrPlacedForAdoptionDate falls in the tax year: the population the adopted-or-placed exception to the time-lived-with-you rule is written about. A child adopted or placed in an earlier year is tested on the ordinary whole-year answer instead. Incomplete while the date is unanswered; its only reader gates on that. Exported because it is the ASKED-WHEN gate for ../writableAdoptedOrPlacedQssLivedWithTpEntireTimeSincePlacement.

Fact.Name: The QSS-specific adopted-or-placed residency exception is met
Fact.Description:
The person was adopted by, or lawfully placed for legal adoption with, the taxpayer during the tax year AND the taxpayer answered that the taxpayer's main home was the person's main home for the ENTIRE time since the adoption or placement. The qualifying-surviving-spouse reading of the adopted-or-placed exception, stricter than the more-than-half standard the dependency rules use. Read only by ../qssPersonResidencyTest.

Fact.Name: Qualifying child of this taxpayer by the section 152(e) special rule
Fact.Description:
The four qualifying-child tests that SURVIVE the special rule for divorced parents, applied to a taxpayer to whom the release moves the child.
WHY THE OTHER FACT WILL NOT DO. ../qualifyingChild requires ../residencyTest, and the whole occasion for IRC 152(e) is that the child did NOT live with the noncustodial parent for more than half the year. Section 152(e)(1) opens "Notwithstanding subsection (c)(1)(B)" - the residency paragraph - and NOTHING ELSE in 152(c) is waived, so this fact re-states ../qualifyingChild with the residency leg replaced by the split Boolean and every other leg kept: the relationship test (152(c)(1)(A) / (c)(2)), the age test (152(c)(1)(C) / (c)(3)), the child's own-support test (152(c)(1)(D)) and the joint-return test (152(c)(1)(E)). It is NOT a re-derivation of ../qualifyingChild: that fact is a different quantity, and both are read side by side under an Any at ../eligibleDependentMinusFilerInformation and ../eligibleCtc.
WHAT IT DOES NOT REACH, stated so the negative is checkable. Head of household, the EITC and the CDCC read the qualifying child "determined without regard to section 152(e)" (IRC 2(b)(1)(A)(i), 32(c)(3)(A)) or say outright that the child is not a qualifying individual of the noncustodial parent (21(e)(5)). No consumer of those three reads this fact.
THE QUALIFYING-RELATIVE LIMB. Section 152(e)(1) also says "or qualifying relative", waiving 152(d)(1)(C). This fact is the qualifying-child limb only; the qualifying-relative limb is ../qualifyingRelativeUnderSection152e, read beside this one.
COMPLETENESS: an unanswered split question the filer reached leaves this fact Incomplete; it is never turned into false. The split Boolean dependentsBenefitSplit:../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc is read through a Switch: answered, it decides; unanswered while ../residencyTest is Complete true, the child lived with the taxpayer more than half the year, so the taxpayer is the custodial parent (IRC 152(e)(4)(A), custody for the greater portion of the year) and the noncustodial route is never reached - false; otherwise the Switch runs off the end and the fact is Incomplete. A kept test that fails (All) still gives Complete false. Its consumers read it bare.

Fact.Name: Qualifying relative of this taxpayer by the section 152(e) special rule
Fact.Description:
The qualifying-relative limb of the special rule for divorced parents: the released child is treated as the noncustodial parent's qualifying RELATIVE when the child is not a qualifying child of anyone because the child fails the qualifying-child age test.
WHO REACHES IT. The custody gate dependentsBenefitSplit:../childMayQualifyForBenefitSplit admits a child under the age of majority where the child lives on July 2 (19 in Alabama and Nebraska, 21 in Mississippi and Puerto Rico) or attested not emancipated, so a released child can be 19 or older at the end of the year, not a student, and fail the 152(c)(3) age test. Without this limb the noncustodial parent holding the release loses the dependency claim and the credit for other dependents the statute gives them.
WHAT IS WAIVED AND WHAT IS KEPT. Section 152(e)(1) waives (c)(1)(B), (c)(4) and (d)(1)(C) only. So the (d)(1)(C) support test is not asked of this taxpayer, while the (d)(1)(B) gross income test (../grossIncomeTest) and the (d)(1)(D) test - the child is not a qualifying child of this or any other taxpayer - stay. The age-test failure makes the child no one's qualifying child on the age leg, and ../isQualifyingChildOfAnother is read fenced for the rest. The relationship test is met by the child definition the split already requires. The dependency exclusions (citizenship, joint return, TIN) are applied where this fact is read, in ../eligibleDependentMinusFilerInformation. The benefit that follows is the credit for other dependents through ../eligibleOdc; ../eligibleCtc stays false (the child is 17 or older).
COMPLETENESS: an unanswered split question the filer reached leaves this fact Incomplete; it is never turned into false. The split Boolean dependentsBenefitSplit:../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsDependencyCtcOdc is read through a Switch: answered, it decides; unanswered while ../residencyTest is Complete true, the child lived with the taxpayer more than half the year, so the taxpayer is the custodial parent (IRC 152(e)(4)(A), custody for the greater portion of the year) and the noncustodial route is never reached - false; otherwise the Switch runs off the end and the fact is Incomplete. A kept test that fails (All) still gives Complete false. Its consumers read it bare.

Fact.Name: EITC Qualifying child
Fact.Description:
Does the child qualify as a QC for EITC? This is mostly the same as the QC test, but omits the support test and has a different residency test.
NO CLAIM CONDITION. IRC 32(c)(3)(A) takes the qualifying child as defined in section 152(c), with no requirement that the taxpayer claim the child as a dependent, so a child the filer could claim but answers not to claim (../tpClaims false) stays an EIC qualifying child. Such a child reaches the unclaimed-EIC-child TIN screens through ../isEITCQCUnclaimedDependent. The claim requirement of the qualifying-child-of-another arm below (the tiebreaker case) is unchanged.
THE MARRIED CHILD. IRC 32(c)(3)(B) keeps a married child only if the taxpayer is ENTITLED to the dependency deduction for the child, "or would be so entitled but for section 152(e)". So the married arm passes on ../eligibleDependent (entitled, whether or not claimed), or when the taxpayer is the custodial parent who released the claim under section 152(e) (dependentsBenefitSplit:../tpCanClaimSplitBenefitsHohEitcCdcc on its custodial-parent arm, not the non-parental arm) and the child meets the citizenship test. Both split reads are fenced.
To-do: take into account QC of another California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (FTB 3514).

The child both qualifies the TP for EITC, and qualifies to increase the amount of EITC they will receive.
EITC qualifying children use different paths for eligibility and calculation. A child may make a taxpayer eligible for the credit, but if they don't have an SSN, they will not increase the amount of the credit - UNLESS the child was born and died in the tax year and the taxpayer attaches the document the Service accepts in the number's place.
THE DOCUMENTED BORN-AND-DIED DISJUNCT. Publication 596 prints the exception in the same CAUTION that states the SSN rule: "To claim a higher EIC amount based on a qualifying child, that qualifying child must have a valid SSN issued on or before the due date of your 2025 return (including extensions), unless the child was born and died in 2025 and you attach to your return a copy of the child's birth certificate, death certificate, or hospital records showing a live birth" - https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p596.pdf, page 13, RIGHT column. Schedule EIC line 2's caption states the same exception - "unless the child was born and died in 2025 or you are claiming the self-only EIC" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f1040sei.pdf, page 1) - and is the only reason the printed "Died" literal goes on that line at all. The bare Code carries no such exception, but neither does IRC 151(e), and the dependents-section substitute this module already computes rests on exactly the same footing: the instruction over the bare statute.
WHY THE DOCUMENTED LEG IS READ BARE, AND IT IS STILL "IsComplete-FIRST". The attestation guard lives INSIDE ../bornAndDiedChildDocumentedInLieuOfTin, not here: every leg of that fact is gated on its own IsComplete (the documentation writable, the deceased flag, the date of birth, and the born-or-died residency screen), so an unasked or unanswered attestation resolves it to Complete FALSE rather than Incomplete. That is why every other consumer - ../eligibleDependentMinusFilerInformation, the two cdcc qualifying-person arms, /knockoutHohQpHasNoTin - reads it bare too, and why wrapping it again here would add a guard that can never fire. An UNDOCUMENTED child therefore stays on the self-only EIC path with the zero-qualifying-child amount, which is the pair of witnesses this fact carries: node-test familyAndHousehold/s252-documented-child-files-and-prints-the-died-literal (Complete 2729.00) against s252-self-only-eic-paid-no-child-ssn (Complete 614.00).
WHAT THIS FIXES ON THE PRINTED RETURN. Schedule EIC line 2 is bound to ../diedLiteralInLieuOfTin, and before this disjunct a documented child could carry "Died" there beside a SELF-ONLY figure on Form 1040 line 27a - which on the caption's own terms is the claim to the higher amount, so the printed pair contradicted itself. It cannot happen now, BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by a second gate: /scheduleEicDependents filters /potentialScheduleEicDependents, whose "none qualify, so list the first one" arm draws from /eitcDependentsCollection = Filter(/familyAndHousehold, eitcQualifyingChild). So a person reaches Schedule EIC line 2 only as an ../eitcQualifyingChild, and a documented born-and-died child who is one is now ALSO a qualifying child for the calculation - the line-2 literal and the one-child rate move together. The child the self-only arm can still list is the one with neither an SSN nor the document, and ../diedLiteralInLieuOfTin is Incomplete for that child, so line 2 is blank. Both halves are pinned in the two witnesses named above (the documented one asserts /eitcDependentsWhoQualify non-empty and diedLiteralInLieuOfTin = Died; the undocumented one asserts /scheduleEicDependents holds the child while diedLiteralInLieuOfTin is Incomplete and /earnedIncomeCredit stays 614.00).
BLAST RADIUS, disclosed rather than designed around: a documented sibling now counts toward /numEitcDependentsCollectionForCalculation, so the self-only suppression's Equal(...,0) conjunct no longer holds on a return that ALSO carries an undocumented born-and-died child, and /knockoutPersonBornAndDiedInTaxYearWithoutTin fires there (node-test familyAndHousehold/born-and-died-two-children-one-documented, false -> true). That is the residual over-refusal class BORNDIED already disclosed, gaining a third pinned instance; widening the conjunct is a redesign the owner ruling does not authorise.

Fact.Name: A non-parent loses the qualifying-child tie-breaker
Fact.Description:
True when the tie-breaker is answered (../nonParentQualifyingChildTieBreakDecided) and it assigns the child to someone else: a parent can claim the child and either a parent does claim the child (IRC 152(c)(4)(A)(i)) or the taxpayer's AGI is not higher than the highest AGI of any parent who can claim the child (IRC 152(c)(4)(C)); or no parent can claim the child and the taxpayer's AGI is not higher than every other claimant's (IRC 152(c)(4)(A)(ii)). The child is then not the taxpayer's qualifying child, so ../eligibleDependentMinusFilerInformation excludes the child, and through the claim requirement on a child who is another taxpayer's qualifying child, so do ../eitcQualifyingChild and ../hohQualifyingPerson.
A TIE IS NOT HIGHER. The statute gives the child to "the taxpayer with the highest adjusted gross income" and, when no parent claims, to another taxpayer "only if" that taxpayer's AGI "is higher than the highest" parent's; an equal AGI is read as not the highest, the reading recorded in the tax interpretations for expert review.
Complete-safe: false outside the population or while an answer is missing.

Fact.Name: A non-parent uses a child who is also another taxpayer's qualifying child

WHY IT REFUSES. IRC 152(c)(4) decides who may use a child two taxpayers could both claim: a parent over a non-parent, and when no parent claims the child, a non-parent only if the non-parent's adjusted gross income is higher than the highest adjusted gross income of any parent (152(c)(4)(C)). The graph asks neither whether a parent is claiming the child nor how the adjusted gross incomes compare, so it cannot tell a lawful claim from one that belongs to the parent. Complete-safe: every read is IsComplete-first, so an unanswered question resolves false.
OVER-BREADTH, disclosed: ../isQualifyingChildOfAnother does not say that the other taxpayer is a PARENT; the refusal also reaches a non-parent whose competing claimant is another non-parent (152(c)(4)(A)(ii), the highest-AGI rule, which is equally unmodelled), and a non-parent whose AGI is in fact higher than every parent's. An intake that would narrow it is not built.

Fact.Name: This person was the taxpayer's spouse at any time during the tax year
Fact.Description:
The taxpayer's answer to whether this person was the taxpayer's spouse at any time during the tax year, even for a single day, and even if the two were divorced, legally separated or living apart by the end of the year.
WHY IT IS ASKED. A person who is not related to the taxpayer in one of the listed ways can still be a qualifying relative by living with the taxpayer all year as a member of the household (../memberOfHouseholdTest). The statute takes one person out of that route by name: someone who at any time during the year was the taxpayer's spouse. Marital status at year end does not decide it, and the rule that treats a spouse living apart as unmarried for filing status does not apply to it. A former spouse who moved back in after a divorce during the year is therefore not a qualifying relative through this route.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION - the application implements this without opening an IRS document.
QUESTION TEXT, with the person's first name substituted for {name}: "At any time in 2025, was {name} your spouse?"
HELP TEXT: "Answer Yes if you and {name} were married to each other on any day in 2025, even if you divorced, separated or stopped living together later in the year. A person who was your spouse at any time during the year can't be your qualifying relative on the basis of living with you."
ASKED WHEN: this person is not related to the taxpayer in one of the listed ways (dependentsRelationship:../qrRelationshipTest is false) and lived with the taxpayer all year, or was born or died during the year (the only cases where the member-of-household route decides the outcome). Ask it once per person.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: no default. Unanswered is not No: ../memberOfHouseholdTest reads this answer bare, so while the member-of-household route is deciding the outcome an unanswered screen leaves that test, and the qualifying-relative claim it feeds, Incomplete rather than granting a dependency the statute may deny. For a person related in a listed way the answer is not needed and its absence changes nothing, because the relationship test passes without the household route.
VALIDATION: Boolean. Yes/No radio, no default selection, answer required to leave the screen.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../memberOfHouseholdTest -> ../relationshipMemberOfHouseholdTest -> ../qualifyingRelative, and from there the dependency claim, the credit for other dependents and the head-of-household and dependent-care qualifying-person chains that read a qualifying relative.

Fact.Name: Member of household test
Fact.Description:
The person meets the member-of-household limb of the qualifying-relative relationship test: the route for a person who is not related to the taxpayer in one of the listed ways.

Fact.Name: EIC's own qualifying-child age test
Fact.Description: The EIC-specific twin of ../ageTest: under 19 and younger than the comparison filer (../eicAgeUnderNineteen), OR a student under 24 on the same calendar-year-of-birth convention (../eicIsAStudentUnder24), OR permanently and totally disabled. Built because Schedule EIC's own printed line 3 fixes the under-19 test to the calendar year of birth ("born after 2006"), a plain comparison of the dependent's birth year against the tax year, while ../ageTest's under-19 and student-under-24 arms apply the day-before-birthday convention for the CTC/ODC and dependency purposes those serve. The two conventions diverge on a child born January 1: the day-before convention adds a year the calendar-year convention does not. Read only by ../eitcRelAgeResJointTest, so the EIC's own qualifying-child determination, and so the credit itself, uses this test rather than the shared one. ../ageTest, ../ageUnderNineteen, ../studentStatusMayAffectBenefits and ../isAStudentUnder24 are UNCHANGED and still serve the CTC/ODC, HOH and dependency purposes that read them.
